title: Processes and process types
sub: Lectures 2–3 · process, performance, process typology, value chain, portfolio, legal issues, location
blurb: What a process is, how to classify yours (it has to be in the video), the value chain, product portfolio, legal duties and outsourcing.
lede: Every exercise in this course starts from a process. Here you learn the one-line definition, the five performance objectives, and the typology the teacher wants to see in your video: where your process sits, what comes before and after it, and which processes support it.
six: A **process** is a set of activities that transforms **input** into **output**.
**Structure follows strategy** (Chandler) and **performance = strategy + operational efficiency** (Porter): operations always cost something, so make them as cost-effective as possible.
Classify a process by production (piece, series, mass), sales order (to order or to stock), technology, layout, location and continuity.
**By time** and **by nature** don't put the process in a box: they place it in the chain (what comes before and after, which processes support it).
Porter's **value chain**: core processes give value to the customer; support processes help the organisation make its margin.
**Outsourcing** = another legal entity; **offshoring** = another geographical region. The two combine independently.
foot: Sources: 3BE216 slides (process typology, Porter's value chain), your Team 02 iPhone 11 deck, and Lecture 3 as recorded (portfolio, legal issues, outsourcing have no slide in the folder).

questions.q: What is a process?
questions.answer: A set of activities that transforms input into output
wrong: A list of the machines in a factory
The organisational chart of the company
A document with requirements and specifications
questions.e: Remember the three words: activities, input, output. The teacher expects this exact definition.

questions.q: Performance equals…
questions.e: Porter: you raise performance through strategy (selling more) and through efficient operations.

questions.q: Can the cost of the operation be cut to zero?
questions.answer: No: an operation always costs something, so make it as cost-effective as possible
wrong: Yes, if sales grow fast enough
questions.e: Operational efficiency can never be zero: you need money to run the operation.

questions.q: 'Structure follows strategy' (Chandler) means…
questions.answer: You can design the operation properly only when the strategy is clear
wrong: The strategy is written after the factory is built
Every company has the same structure
Marketing decides the layout of the factory
questions.e: First the strategy, then the structure (the operation) that serves it.

questions.q: Few products (5–10 references) in a very big volume is…
questions.e: Low variety, high volume = mass.

questions.q: A tailor making a suit for each customer is…
questions.e: One product, different for every customer: piece production.

questions.q: A factory makes several types of screens (not one per customer) in good volume. That is…
questions.e: The lecture's screen factory: a decent range, good volume, not one per customer → series.

questions.q: A call centre answering the same internet question for thousands of customers is…
questions.e: Many people asking for the same thing = mass service. Consulting, unique for every client, is a professional service.

questions.q: You manufacture first, then the products wait in a warehouse to be sold. That is…
questions.e: To stock: produce, then sell. To order: wait for the email, call or customer, then start.

questions.q: Which is true about mechanical and chemical processes?
questions.answer: A chemical reaction is hard to reverse; a bent piece of metal can be bent back
wrong: Mechanical processes can never be reversed
Yogurt and wine are mechanical processes
questions.e: Bending is reversible; a chemical reaction mostly isn't. Yogurt, beer and wine are biochemical.

questions.q: In a grouped layout, when is grouping by product better than grouping by technology?
questions.answer: When you make only a few products
wrong: When you make many different products
questions.e: Few products (closer to mass) → by product. Many products (closer to piece) → by technology.

questions.q: Airbus A380: wings from Spain, fuselage from Germany, final assembly in France. Which layout?
questions.e: Big products are made in phases: think of a plane, a boat or a building.

questions.q: A food truck or a building site is a … process.
questions.e: The 'factory' goes to the customer or the site: mobile.

questions.q: The customer service of a global airline that can never be switched off is…
questions.e: It runs 24/7. A metal-industry oven is the same: it can't be switched off for the weekend.

questions.q: What does classifying a process 'by time' tell you?
questions.answer: Where it sits in the chain: what comes before it and what comes after it
wrong: How many hours a day it runs
Whether it can be stopped at night
questions.e: By time (pre-production, production, post-production) and by nature (core, support, service) place your process in the chain. Many videos get this wrong.

questions.q: The workers' canteen in a chair factory is a…
questions.e: Not your business, but you still have to manage it: bad food makes workers ill.

questions.q: Maintenance of the cold saw on a wood-cutting line is a…
questions.e: It helps the core process (cutting wood) to work.

questions.q: Which is a SUPPORT activity in Porter's value chain?
questions.e: Support: firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development, procurement.

questions.q: Outsourcing means…
questions.answer: another legal entity does the work for you
wrong: the customer does part of the work
questions.e: Out = out of your legal entity. It can be at home or abroad.

questions.q: Offshoring means…
questions.answer: the work is done in another geographical region
wrong: another legal entity does the work
the work is done at night
questions.e: Off-shore = another region. You can be insourced offshore (your own factory abroad) or outsourced at home.

questions.q: Why do firms reshore (bring production back)?
questions.answer: Logistics and coordination costs grow and wages abroad rise
questions.e: From Lecture 3: the labour gap shrinks while logistics and coordination costs eat the margin.

questions.q: A product made in Czechia has labels only in Czech. Can you sell it in Germany?
questions.answer: No: the information has to be in German
wrong: Yes, the EU has one market
Yes, if the product is certified
questions.e: From Lecture 3: you must comply with the rules of the region, including the language.

questions.q: First-pass yield and rework rate measure which performance objective?
questions.e: From your iPhone deck: Q = first-pass yield, defects, rework rate.

vocab.meaning: A set of activities that transforms input into output.
Quality, Speed, Dependability, Flexibility, Cost (Q-S-D-F-C).
One or very few of each product, different for each customer (a tailor).
A decent range of products in a good, not huge, volume.
Few products in a very big volume.
One product made all the time in huge volume (water, electricity).
A service that is unique for every client (consulting, IT projects).
Many customers get the same service (a call centre).
You start working when the order (email, call, customer) arrives.
You produce first; the products wait in a warehouse to be sold.
One workstation where one person has everything at hand.
Workstations one after the other; each does one step.
Areas grouped by product (few products) or by technology (many products).
A big product is made in phases (a plane, a boat, a building).
The process moves to the customer or site (a food truck, a building site).
The process can be stopped and started again (weekends).
Activities that give value to the customer: what the customer pays for.
Activities that help the core process work (machine maintenance).
Not your business, but you manage it (canteen, coffee, gardening).
Porter (1985): core and support activities that together create the margin.
The offer of the organisation: everything it sells.
Products that share components in production (motors, metal sheets, platforms).
Another legal entity does the work for you.
The work is done in another geographical region.
Bringing production back home when the total cost abroad gets too high.

facts: A process is a set of activities that transforms input into {output|profit|structure|strategy}.
Few products in a very big volume is {mass|piece|series|project} production.
A food truck is an example of a {mobile|immobile|continuous|flow} process.
Grouping the layout by product makes sense when you make {few|many|mobile|unique} products.
Maintenance of the machines is a {support|core|service|post-production} process.
Porter published the value chain in {1985|1960|2012|1969}.
sheet: piece · series · mass (book: project, jobbing, batch, mass, continuous)
individual · flow · group (by product or technology) · phase
